sources.reviewed_text_2: A general textbook on designed experiments, reviewed privately with project_text.py

nodes.name: Experiment
nodes.definition: Intentionally disturbing a system by changing factors, to learn cause and effect.
nodes.quote: In order to learn about a system, we have to disturb it and change it. This is to ensure cause and effect.

nodes.name: Run
nodes.definition: One experiment in a set: eight experiments are eight runs.
nodes.quote: When we perform an experiment, we call it a run.

nodes.name: Response
nodes.definition: The measured outcome of a run, written y. It must always be measurable in some way.
nodes.quote: An important aspect about the outcome is that it is always measurable--in some way.

nodes.name: Qualitative outcome
nodes.definition: An outcome described in categories, such as pass or fail, or a colour.
nodes.quote: A qualitative outcome might also be a description of what happened, for example,

nodes.name: Objective
nodes.definition: An outcome together with what you want of it: maximize, minimize, or keep the same.
nodes.quote: which combines an outcome and the need to adjust that outcome.

nodes.name: Factor
nodes.definition: The thing you can change to influence the outcome.
nodes.quote: is the thing you can change to influence the outcome.

nodes.name: Numeric factor
nodes.definition: A factor with ordered, measured values, such as 15 mL or 30 mL of water.
nodes.quote: Numeric factors are quantified by measuring, such as giving 15 mL of water or 30 mL of water to the plant each day.

nodes.name: Categorical factor
nodes.definition: A factor with a few values that have no order, such as soil A or soil B.
nodes.quote: Categorical factors usually take on a limited number of values.

nodes.name: Level
nodes.definition: A setting of a factor in a design, such as its low (-1) or high (+1) value.
nodes.quote: In this section we consider the case when these factors are at two levels.

nodes.name: Cause and effect
nodes.definition: A change in a factor that produces a change in the response; shown only by intentional manipulation.
nodes.quote: you must disturb your system, and then observe it. This is the principle of causality, or

nodes.name: Happenstance data
nodes.definition: Everyday operating data, collected without intentional changes to the system; it is confounded by other events, so it cannot be relied on to imply cause and effect.
nodes.quote: That is why happenstance data cannot be relied on to imply cause and effect.

nodes.name: Feedback control
nodes.definition: Control systems keep operation in a small zone, so the data they produce carry little information.
nodes.quote: Feedback control systems keep the region of operation to a small zone.

nodes.name: Correlation
nodes.definition: Two variables moving together. Some association is usually present when there is a causal link, but on its own it is not sufficient evidence of causality.
nodes.quote: some observable association is usually present when there is a causal link, but the association on its own is not sufficient evidence of it.

nodes.name: Learning cycle
nodes.definition: Conjecture, expected consequences, experiment and data, then a new or revised conjecture.
nodes.quote: learning from and improving a system is an iterative process. It usually follows this cycle:

nodes.name: Conjecture
nodes.definition: A hypothesis believed true, whose consequences an experiment tests.
nodes.quote: Make a conjecture (hypothesis), which we believe is true.

nodes.name: Troubleshooting
nodes.definition: Experimenting to fix a problem, which also shows how the system works.
nodes.quote: One of the most frequent reasons we experiment is to fix a problem with our process.

nodes.name: Disturbance
nodes.definition: A variable that affects y but is not of interest: operators, ambient conditions, equipment, lab analyses, time.
nodes.quote: Operators, ambient conditions, physical equipment, lab analyses, and time-dependent effects (catalyst deactivation, fouling), will impact the response.

nodes.name: Controlled disturbance
nodes.definition: A disturbance held constant for all runs, so its effect cancels out.
nodes.quote: in which case it isn't a disturbance anymore, as it is held constant for all experiments, and its effect cancels out.

nodes.name: Time-dependent effect
nodes.definition: Slow changes such as catalyst deactivation or fouling that affect the response over time.
nodes.quote: and time-dependent effects (catalyst deactivation, fouling), will impact the response.

nodes.name: Randomization
nodes.definition: Running experiments in random order so unknown disturbances cannot systematically affect the response.
nodes.quote: experiments must be performed in random order to avoid any unmeasured, and uncontrolled, disturbances from impacting the system.

nodes.name: Randomization test
nodes.definition: Compare the observed difference with the differences from every possible reassignment of the A and B labels.
nodes.quote: Fisher's insight was to create one long vector of these outcomes

nodes.name: Pairing
nodes.definition: Running two experiments on the same subject and analysing their difference, so a shared disturbance cancels.
nodes.quote: pairing is when two experiments are run on the same subject and we analyze the differences in the two response values, rather than the actual response values.

nodes.name: Comparing two conditions
nodes.definition: Comparing condition A with B using a pooled variance and a confidence interval for the difference.
nodes.quote: We first calculate a pooled variance, then a

nodes.name: Pooled variance
nodes.definition: A combined variance estimate from two groups, used in the z-value for their difference.
nodes.quote: which already assumes the spread at level A equals the spread at level B.

nodes.name: Indicator variable
nodes.definition: A 0/1 variable that codes condition A or B in a least squares model.
nodes.quote: is an indicator variable. For example,

nodes.name: Confidence interval
nodes.definition: A range for an effect; the effect is statistically significant when the interval does not span zero.
nodes.quote: significant effect when this confidence interval does not span zero.

nodes.name: t-distribution
nodes.definition: The reference distribution for a difference or a coefficient divided by its standard error.
nodes.quote: from the data (rather than known), this statistic is strictly

nodes.name: Null hypothesis
nodes.definition: The statement a test takes as true until the data give evidence against it; for A versus B, that there is no difference between them.
nodes.quote: We do this because the null hypothesis, the statement a test takes as true until the data give evidence against it, is that there is no difference between A and B.

nodes.name: Statistical significance
nodes.definition: An effect is statistically significant when its confidence interval does not span zero; without replicates, Lenth's margin of error gives an objective cutoff instead.
nodes.quote: There are three ways to judge whether a main effect or interaction is significant.

nodes.name: Practical significance
nodes.definition: Whether an effect is large enough to matter, judged from the interval's width and the process variance.
nodes.quote: However, the width of this interval and how symmetrically it spans zero can cause us to come to a different,

nodes.name: Changing one single variable at a time
nodes.definition: Changing one factor at a time, in a search or a fixed design: interactions go unestimated, effects are less precise than a factorial's, and a search can stop at a suboptimal point.
nodes.quote: is not an efficient way for experimentation. Note that OFAT is an alternative name for COST

nodes.name: False optimum
nodes.definition: A point that looks best when factors are changed one at a time, but is not the optimum.
nodes.quote: Changing one single variable at a time leads you into thinking you've reached the optimum, when all you've done in fact is trap yourself at a suboptimal solution.

nodes.name: Order dependence
nodes.definition: With COST the result depends on which factor is changed first.
nodes.quote: This is very unsatisfactory: we cannot use methods to optimize our processes that depend on the order of experiments!

nodes.name: Designed experiment
nodes.definition: A planned set of runs; with several factors it changes them simultaneously, often needing fewer runs than COST, and gives the same result whatever the run order.
nodes.quote: Designed experiments are always run in random order -- as we will presently see -- and we will get the same result, no matter the order.

nodes.name: Full factorial
nodes.definition: Every combination of the factors' levels; factors may have different numbers of levels (3 x 2 x 2 = 12 runs). At two levels each, 2^k runs for k factors.
nodes.quote: the :math:`2` refers to the number of levels for each factor

nodes.name: Coding
nodes.definition: Centering and scaling a factor; the standard form is (value - center)/(range/2), so low is -1 and high is +1.
nodes.quote: It is standard practice to represent the data from designed experiments in a centered and scaled form:

nodes.name: Standard order
nodes.definition: Writing runs with the first factor's sign alternating fastest and the last slowest.
nodes.quote: which alternates the sign of the first variable the fastest and the last variable the slowest.

nodes.name: Choosing the factor range
nodes.definition: Choose low and high at the edges of normal operation, not at the extreme values a factor could take.
nodes.quote: The general guidance is to choose the low and high values at the edges of normal operation.

nodes.name: Cube plot
nodes.definition: The design drawn as a square or cube with the response written at each corner.
nodes.quote: For simple systems you can visualize the design and results

nodes.name: Main effect
nodes.definition: The average change in y when a factor moves from its low to its high level.
nodes.quote: The effects are considered, by convention, to be the difference from the high level to the low level.

nodes.name: Interaction
nodes.definition: When the effect of one factor depends on the level of another. Interactions are symmetric.
nodes.quote: In summary, interaction means the effect of one factor depends on the level of the other factor.

nodes.name: Two-factor interaction
nodes.definition: The interaction of two factors, such as T x S.
nodes.quote: What is missing is an interaction term, given by the product of temperature and substrate.

nodes.name: Three-factor interaction
nodes.definition: The interaction of three factors; seldom large in real systems.
nodes.quote: Very very seldom do three-factor interactions occur, nor are they often of practical significance.

nodes.name: Interaction plot
nodes.definition: The response against one factor, a line per level of another; lines that are not parallel show interaction.
nodes.quote: The lack of parallel lines is a clear indication of interaction.

nodes.name: Least squares model
nodes.definition: y = Xb + e, fitted with b = (X'X)^-1 X'y. It works even when the design was not run exactly as planned.
nodes.quote: whether the experimental design was executed accurately or not: the least squares model always works

nodes.name: Model matrix X
nodes.definition: One row per run and one column per model term, with a column of ones for the intercept.
found_as: table of plus and minus signs
nodes.quote: Each row is one experimental run; each column is one term in the model.

nodes.name: Orthogonality
nodes.definition: The columns of X are mutually orthogonal, so X'X is diagonal and each coefficient is estimated and interpreted separately. Quadratic columns, which correlate with the intercept, are checked for orthogonality after centring.
nodes.quote: matrix has only zeros on the off-diagonals: it indicates that matrix

nodes.name: Intercept
nodes.definition: The model's constant b0; for a coded factorial, the average of the runs and the predicted center point.
nodes.quote: Notice from the least squares equations how it is just the average of the four experimental values, even though we did not actually perform an experiment at the center.

nodes.name: Coefficient
nodes.definition: A parameter of the fitted model, one per term; for a coded factor's main effect it is the change in y per coded unit, over half the factor's range.
nodes.quote: They are the same, as long as we are careful to interpret them as the change over

nodes.name: Keep the parent main effects
nodes.definition: If an interaction is significant, keep in the model every main effect that it is made of.
nodes.quote: Also, if you conclude the interaction term is significant, then you must also include all main factors that make up that interaction term in the model.

nodes.name: Read main effects with their interactions
nodes.definition: A main effect cannot be interpreted on its own when it takes part in a significant interaction.
nodes.quote: We cannot interpret the main effects separately from the interaction effects

nodes.name: Robustness
nodes.definition: A small effect means y is insensitive to that factor: y is robust to changes in it.
nodes.quote: This is desirable in some situations. It means we can adjust that

nodes.name: Degrees of freedom
nodes.definition: Independent values in a sum of squares. With n runs, p parameters and m distinct factor combinations (i-th run n_i times): residual n-p = pure error sum(n_i-1) + lack of fit m-p.
nodes.quote: If there are more experiments than parameters to be estimated, then we have extra degrees of freedom.

nodes.name: Replicate
nodes.definition: One run repeated in full: setup, running the experiment and measuring the result. A design run twice has every run replicated; other texts call one such pass a replicate.
nodes.quote: A replicate is one run repeated in full: system setup, running the experiment and measuring the result

nodes.name: Repeat measurement
nodes.definition: Measuring one sample twice; it estimates only measurement error and is not a true replicate.
nodes.quote: is not a true replicate. That is only an estimate of the measurement error and analytical error.

nodes.name: Center point
nodes.definition: A run with every factor at coded 0. It checks overall curvature and, replicated, estimates pure error, but cannot tell which factor curves; in a factorial it keeps X orthogonal.
nodes.quote: Note that the center point runs do not change the orthogonality of

nodes.name: Standard error
nodes.definition: The spread of an estimate such as a coefficient: its estimated standard deviation. In a coded orthogonal design, S_E(b) = sqrt(S_E^2 / sum x^2), with S_E the estimated noise standard deviation.
nodes.quote: the standard error for coefficient :math:`b_i` is :math:`S_E(b_i) = \sqrt{\mathcal{V}\left(b_i\right)} = \sqrt{\dfrac{S_E^2}{\sum{x_i^2}}}`

nodes.name: Noise standard deviation
nodes.definition: The run-to-run scatter of the response with every factor held fixed, sigma; its estimate S_E comes from replicate runs, residual degrees of freedom or external data.
nodes.quote: There are no degrees of freedom left to estimate the noise standard deviation, the run-to-run scatter of the response when every factor is held fixed.

nodes.name: Pareto plot
nodes.definition: Absolute coefficients in sorted order, intercept left out; significance judged by eye. Needs coded factors.
nodes.quote: then plot as shown the absolute value of the model coefficients in sorted order, from largest magnitude to smallest, ignoring the intercept term.

nodes.name: Significance from standard errors
nodes.definition: Report each effect with its standard error; it is significant when effect +/- c_t x SE excludes zero.
nodes.quote: However, it is customary to just report the standard error next to the coefficients, so that users can apply their own level of confidence.

nodes.name: Refit without small effects
nodes.definition: Drop clearly small effects to gain degrees of freedom, then estimate the error and check the residuals.
nodes.quote: After having established which effects are significant, we can exclude the nonsignificant effects and increase the degrees of freedom.

nodes.name: Residual analysis
nodes.definition: Residuals plotted in run order, against fitted values, and on a q-q plot.
nodes.quote: Plots of the residuals in experimental order, against fitted values, q-q plots and all the other assessment tools from earlier are used, as usual.

nodes.name: Factorial efficiency
nodes.definition: A factorial halves a main effect's variance versus COST, partly by using more runs; those same runs also estimate the other effects and interactions at no additional cost.
nodes.quote: whereas the COST comparison uses only two, so part of the variance reduction is simply the extra runs.

nodes.name: Missing values
nodes.definition: Responses lost from some runs. Main effects can often still be estimated; if the least squares model was saturated, drop higher-order interaction terms to get a square system.
nodes.quote: if the least squares model was saturated, it becomes an underdetermined system: more unknowns than equations

nodes.name: Off-target run
nodes.definition: A run set to a level other than planned. Code its actual value and fit by least squares; X is then almost orthogonal.
nodes.quote: will not be a diagonal matrix, but it will be almost diagonal.

nodes.name: Fractional factorial
nodes.definition: A fraction of a full factorial's runs, chosen systematically by generators rather than at random. At two levels per factor, 2^(k-p) runs for k factors.
nodes.quote: In general, we can run a :math:`2^{k-p}` fractional factorial.

nodes.name: Half fraction
nodes.definition: Half of a full factorial: 2^(k-1) runs.
nodes.quote: So this is our half-factorial designed experiment in 3 factors, but it only requires 4 experiments as shown by the open points in the figure.

nodes.name: Quarter fraction
nodes.definition: A quarter of a full factorial: 2^(k-2) runs.
nodes.quote: while a :math:`2^{k-2}` design is a quarter fraction, and so on.

nodes.name: Complementary half fraction
nodes.definition: The other half of a full factorial, made by flipping the sign of the generator.
nodes.quote: This complementary fraction is found by flipping the sign on the generating factor.

nodes.name: Saturated design
nodes.definition: A design with one run per estimated term, such as 7 factors in 8 runs; usually resolution III.
nodes.quote: is one in which the number of runs equals the number of parameters being estimated, so there are **no degrees of freedom left over**.

nodes.name: Plackett-Burman design
nodes.definition: A screening design in any multiple of 4 runs from 12: 12, 16, 20, 24, ...
nodes.quote: Plackett-Burman designs are screening designs that can be run in any multiple of 4

nodes.name: Confounding
nodes.definition: Two effects cannot be separated, so their coefficient estimates their sum.
nodes.quote: the least-squares coefficient is a sum of both these effects.

nodes.name: Alias structure
nodes.definition: The list of aliases of every effect in a design.
nodes.quote: Calculating which main effects and two-factor interactions will be confounded with each other, called the

nodes.name: Collinearity
nodes.definition: A column of X equal to another column, or to a linear combination of others (perfect collinearity), so X'X is singular and cannot be inverted.
nodes.quote: because one or more columns are exactly identical to another column, also known as

nodes.name: Generator
nodes.definition: Assigning an extra factor to an interaction column, such as D = ABC.
nodes.quote: This is called the *generating relation* for the design.

nodes.name: Word
nodes.definition: A product of factor letters equal to I, such as ABD.
nodes.quote: The generator terms such as **ABD** and **ACE** are called

nodes.name: Defining relation
nodes.definition: All the words equal to I, found from the products of the generators: 2^p words.
nodes.quote: factorial design is produced by :math:`p` generators and has a defining relationship of :math:`2^p` words.

nodes.name: Identity column I
nodes.definition: The column of ones. Any factor times itself is I.
nodes.quote: A factor multiplied by itself is the identity, or intercept column

nodes.name: Finding aliases
nodes.definition: Multiply an effect by the defining relation to list what it is aliased with.
nodes.quote: can be found quickly by multiplying the effect we are interested in by the defining relationship.

nodes.name: Reassign factors to letters
nodes.definition: Choose which real factor gets which letter to obtain the least harmful confounding.
nodes.quote: then just reassign the factors to the letters to achieve the "least-worst" confounding for your situation.

nodes.name: Resolution
nodes.definition: The length of the shortest word in the defining relation, written as a Roman numeral.
nodes.quote: of a design is given by the length of the shortest word in the defining relation.

nodes.name: Resolution III
nodes.definition: Shortest defining word has three letters: main effects are not confounded with each other but are aliased with two-factor interactions. Good for screening.
nodes.quote: Main effects are not confounded with each other.

nodes.name: Resolution IV
nodes.definition: Main effects are clear of two-factor interactions, which are aliased with each other. Good for characterizing.
nodes.quote: Main effects are not aliased with two-factor interactions either

nodes.name: Resolution V
nodes.definition: Shortest word in the defining relation has five letters: no main effect or two-factor interaction is aliased with another, but two-factor interactions are aliased with three-factor interactions.
nodes.quote: But two-factor interactions are aliased with three-factor interactions

nodes.name: Trade-off table
nodes.definition: Resolution against number of factors and runs (Box, Hunter and Hunter, p 272).
nodes.quote: You can use the following table to visualize the trade-off between design resolution, the number of factors

nodes.name: Projectivity
nodes.definition: A design of resolution R contains a full factorial in any R - 1 factors.
nodes.quote: contains an embedded full factorial using a combination of any 3 factors

nodes.name: Foldover
nodes.definition: Running a second fraction with signs switched, then analysing both fractions together.
nodes.quote: Now consider putting all 16 runs together and analyzing the joint results.

nodes.name: Single-factor foldover
nodes.definition: Switch the signs of one factor to de-alias it and its two-factor interactions.
nodes.quote: switching the sign of one factor will de-alias that factor's main effect, and all its associated two-factor interactions

nodes.name: Full foldover
nodes.definition: Switch all signs to raise a resolution III design to resolution IV.
nodes.quote: Its shortest word now has four letters, so this is a

nodes.name: Sequential experimentation
nodes.definition: Experiments are run in stages, each designed from what the last one revealed.
nodes.quote: Experiments are not a one-shot operation. They are almost always sequential, as we learn more and more about our system.

nodes.name: Screening
nodes.definition: Finding the few important factors among many candidates.
nodes.quote: to separate out the important factors from the many potential factors.

nodes.name: Few large effects
nodes.definition: Only a few of the many factors studied drive most of the variation in the response: the experimental form of the Pareto principle.
nodes.quote: The principle of effect sparsity states that only a few of the many factors studied drive most of the variation in the response.

nodes.name: Blocking
nodes.definition: Running the experiment in groups so a known disturbance affects the response without misleading the results.
nodes.quote: blocking is a special way of running the experiment so that the disturbance actually does affect the response, but we construct the experiment so that this effect is not misleading.

nodes.name: Block
nodes.definition: A group of runs made under one level of a disturbance, such as one batch of material. Runs within a block are randomized.
nodes.quote: The experiments within each block must be run randomly.

nodes.name: Block generator
nodes.definition: The interaction the block effect is confounded with, such as block = ABC.
nodes.quote: to confound the two blocks of experiments with the 3-factor interaction, **ABC**.

nodes.name: Block on the highest interaction
nodes.definition: When splitting a 2^k factorial into two blocks, confound the block effect with the highest possible interaction. With more blocks, keep all block contrasts, including products, off main effects.
nodes.quote: You should always confound your block effect on the highest possible interaction term.

nodes.name: Response surface methods
nodes.definition: A sequence of local empirical models of one or more responses, fitted to map how the factors affect them, to meet specifications, or to move the process towards an optimum.
nodes.quote: RSM is a way to explore the effect of operating conditions (the factors) on the response variable

nodes.name: Response surface
nodes.definition: The unknown surface of y over the factors' space.
nodes.quote: As we map out the unknown response surface of

nodes.name: Steepest ascent
nodes.definition: Move all factors in proportion to their main-effect coefficients, in coded units: delta x_i = (b_i / b_A) delta x_A. Useful while main effects are large compared with interactions, curvature and noise.
nodes.quote: it is a useful direction to climb while the main effects are large compared with the two-factor interactions, the curvature and the noise

nodes.name: Step size
nodes.definition: Big enough to change the response in a few runs, small enough not to jump over the optimum.
nodes.quote: big enough to cause a change in the response in a reasonable number of experiments, but not so big as to miss an optimum.

nodes.name: Return to the last best point
nodes.definition: When the response drops, go back to the best run and fit a new factorial around it.
nodes.quote: So we return back to our *last best point*, because the surface has obviously changed, and we should refit our model with a new factorial in this neighbourhood

nodes.name: Curvature
nodes.definition: A bend in the response surface; every optimum has it, and a linear model cannot describe it.
nodes.quote: An optimum exhibits curvature, so a model that only has linear terms in it will not be suitable

nodes.name: Checking for curvature
nodes.definition: Compare the model's predicted center point, b0, with the measured center point.
nodes.quote: Curvature can be assessed by comparing the predicted center point, i.e. the model's intercept

nodes.name: Quadratic model
nodes.definition: Outside mixtures, a model with squared terms such as b_TT x_T^2, to describe curvature. A mixture's second-order Scheffe model has none: they fold into its cross-products.
nodes.quote: the pure quadratics add nothing and must be left out.

nodes.name: Central composite design
nodes.definition: A factorial plus center points plus axial points; fits a quadratic model.
nodes.quote: If there is curvature, add axial points to expand the factorial into a central composite design.

nodes.name: Axial point
nodes.definition: Outside mixture designs, a central composite design run with one factor off-centre and the rest at 0: about 1.4 coded units out for 2 factors, 1.7 for 3 (rotatable); ±1 face-centred.
nodes.quote: coded units away from the center for a 2 factor system

nodes.name: Box-Behnken design
nodes.definition: A three-level response surface design for the full quadratic model with no runs at the cube corners; suits infeasible corners but cannot be built sequentially from a factorial.
nodes.quote: A BBD places no runs at the cube vertices: there is no run with every

nodes.name: Contour plot
nodes.definition: Lines of equal predicted response, used to choose where to run next.
nodes.quote: Draw contour plots of this estimated response surface

nodes.name: Optimum
nodes.definition: The allowed settings with the best response. The surface is flat at an optimum inside the region, but need not be at one on a constraint.
nodes.quote: An optimum on a constraint, at the edge of that region, need not be flat

nodes.name: Response levels off
nodes.definition: Successive steps give little improvement.
nodes.quote: The response variable will start to plateau, since, recall that the first derivative is zero at an optimum

nodes.name: Response drops
nodes.definition: The response falls, sometimes fast, after a step: you overshot the optimum.
nodes.quote: The response variable decreases, sometimes very rapidly, because we have overshot the optimum.

nodes.name: Interactions as large as main effects
nodes.definition: Interaction terms similar to or larger than the main effects.
nodes.quote: The two-factor interaction terms become similar to, or larger than, the main effect terms.

nodes.name: Center point far from prediction
nodes.definition: The measured center point differs from the predicted center point, b0, by an amount that is large compared with the model's effects.
nodes.quote: indicates the response surface is curved.

nodes.name: Near an optimum
nodes.definition: The region where the surface bends, so a linear model no longer points the way.
nodes.quote: An optimum exhibits curvature, so a model that only has linear terms in it will not be suitable to use to find the direction of steepest ascent

nodes.name: Several responses
nodes.definition: Two or more outcomes that trade off, such as production rate and energy.
nodes.quote: For example we can achieve a higher production rate, but it is at the expense of more energy.

nodes.name: Combine into one response
nodes.definition: Rewrite the outcomes as one y, such as total cost or net profit.
nodes.quote: One way to balance all competing objectives is to rephrase the

nodes.name: Overlay the response surfaces
nodes.definition: Superimpose the contours of each response so the trade-offs can be seen.
nodes.quote: This is tremendously helpful when discussing and evaluating alternate operating points, because plant managers and operators can then visually see the trade-offs.

nodes.name: Categorical factors in RSM
nodes.definition: Fix a categorical factor, optimize the rest, then try its other value.
nodes.quote: are handled by fixing them at one or the other value, and then performing the optimization conditional on those selected values.

nodes.name: Evolutionary operation
nodes.definition: Small, repeated factorial perturbations on a full-scale process to keep it at its moving optimum.
nodes.quote: EVOP is an iterative hunt for the process optimum by making small perturbations to the system.

nodes.name: Process drift
nodes.definition: The optimum moves as heat exchangers foul, catalyst deactivates, and raw materials change.
nodes.quote: Since the process is not constant, the optimum will gradually move away from its current operating point.

nodes.name: Phase 1: screening
nodes.definition: Put as many factors as possible into as few runs as possible, with a saturated or Plackett-Burman design.
nodes.quote: Include as many factors into as few runs as possible. Use a saturated, resolution III design, or a Plackett and Burman design.

nodes.name: Phase 2: sequential runs
nodes.definition: Add runs to the first ones: foldover, projectivity, and fractions of higher resolution.
nodes.quote: The **second phase** is to add *sequential experiments* to the previous experiments.

nodes.name: Phase 3: optimization
nodes.definition: Explore the response surface of the important factors, then add curvature terms near the optimum.
nodes.quote: Once you reach the optimum, then second order effects and curvature must be added to assess the direction of the optimum.

nodes.name: Phase 4: maintain the optimum
nodes.definition: Keep hunting for the moving optimum with evolutionary operation.
nodes.quote: You should be always hunting for the process optimum.

nodes.name: Spend 25% first
nodes.definition: Spend no more than 20% to 25% of time and budget on the first group of experiments.
nodes.quote: do not spend more than 20% to 25% of your time and budget on your first group of experiments.

nodes.name: The best time to run an experiment
nodes.definition: The best time to run an experiment is after the experiment: you always learn what you wish you had done.
nodes.quote: The best time to run an experiment is after the experiment.

nodes.name: Run the center point first
nodes.definition: The first run often fails while you learn the protocol; make it a center point, which the analysis does not need.
nodes.quote: Since the center point is not required to analyze the data, it is worth using that first run to learn about your system.

nodes.name: Constraint
nodes.definition: A limit on which runs are allowed or which results are acceptable: a bound on a factor, an unsafe combination of factors, or a response specification (a minimum purity).
nodes.quote: lower or upper bounds on an ingredient cut the simplex down to a smaller region inside it

nodes.name: Lost orthogonality
nodes.definition: Moving a run to obey a constraint makes X no longer orthogonal and shrinks the region the design spans.
nodes.quote: We have lost orthogonality. We have also reduced the space

nodes.name: Optimal design
nodes.definition: Runs chosen by a computer to optimize a criterion, for a model you specify, subject to constraints.
nodes.quote: select the experimental runs by optimizing some criterion,

nodes.name: Candidate set

nodes.quote: the chart draws limits at plus and minus two standard errors for a range of such values

nodes.name: Dispersion effect
nodes.definition: The change a factor makes to the spread of the response, not its average; with replicated runs it shows as more scatter at one level than at the other.
nodes.quote: A factor can change the spread of the response and not only its average.

nodes.name: Orthogonal blocking
nodes.definition: Dividing a design into blocks so that the block effect is orthogonal to every model term; a shift between blocks then leaves the coefficients unchanged.

nodes.name: Simplex-centroid design
nodes.definition: The simplex-lattice runs plus the overall centroid: seven runs for three ingredients, each pure component, each two-way blend and the equal blend of all three.
nodes.quote: `simplex-centroid design` in three ingredients.
